items.content_snippet: Samuel Yeboah , Francesco Di Chiara and Mingliang Liu Today, Netflix runs two Flink autoscalers. That is exactly one more than we want. The second came from the Apache Flink community, and it can scale workloads our homegrown system was never designed for. items.title: The Missing Layer: Design Taste in AI Agents — Hassan El Mghari, Together AI
items.content_snippet: Most people can spot a vibe coded app in two seconds and cannot say why. Hassan El Mghari names it: the purple gradient background, italics in the header, a scroll to explore prompt nobody asked for, all caps pills with wide letter spacing, too many emoji. He reckons you could list thirty such tells, and naming them is what lets you tell an agent to avoid them. items.title: Agentic SDLC at Uber — Uday Kiran Medisetty & Adam Huda, Uber
items.content_snippet: More than 70% of pull requests at Uber now come from local or cloud agents, and lines of code per engineer has doubled year over year. Uday Kiran Medisetty walks through the six pieces of infrastructure underneath that, and the constraint shaping all of them shows up in the first one: every model call in the company goes through a single gateway doing Spire identity, redaction of 20 plus PII types, and five specialized safety models, with that entire guardrail budget held under 100 milliseconds.

items.title: Unlock Agent Autonomy: The Runtime for AI-Native Systems — Tushar Jain, Docker
items.content_snippet: An agent that had quietly emailed him a nightly summary for weeks decided one morning to post it as a pull request instead. Nothing had changed. The model simply judged that publishing would be more helpful. The report held Tushar Jain's own notes on how his team was working, which is precisely the sort of thing he did not want landing in a repo. items.title: Your Fine-Tuned Model Is Tech Debt: A 50x ROI House of Cards — Dan Bjornn, Lease End
items.content_snippet: A customer replied good morning to an outreach text and the model called him immediately. Another confirmed a Thursday appointment, said sounds good, and was told a call was happening right now. Both reached production, from a finetuned classifier that had also generated $12 million of revenue at 50 times return inside a year. items.title: How I automate my own job at Hugging Face using agents — Niels Rogge, Hugging Face
items.content_snippet: Thousands of GitHub issues, opened automatically, have produced exactly two negative replies. Niels Rogge works on what he calls the Google Drive to the hub team at Hugging Face, whose job is noticing that a paper's weights are sitting on Dropbox or Zenodo where nobody will find them, then asking the authors to publish on the hub instead. Hundreds of papers land on arXiv every day, so he automated himself. The useful part is that he built it twice, in opposite shapes, and explains why each time.

items.title: Prototyping as Leadership: How a CTO Ships with AI Agents — Hursh Agrawal, The Browser Company

It was not possible a year ago. items.title: The Last Human Code Review: Building Trust in AI-Generated Code — Itamar Friedman, Qodo
items.content_snippet: If you are shipping AI generated code faster than your humans can review it, Itamar Friedman's position is that you are inside the problem rather than ahead of it. He asks the room whether developers will still be reading diffs line by line by the end of the year, then reports finding two incompatible camps among engineering leaders the night before: one holding that every line must be human trusted, the other content to ship bugs and fix them quickly because velocity wins.
